mentions.text: PLUM consists of item tokenization using Semantic IDs (Rajput et al., 2023; Singh et al., 2024), continued pre-training (CPT) on domain-specific data, and task-specific fine-tuning for recommendation objectives.

Despite the use of neural networks, the dominant paradigm in industrial recommenders continues to rely on massive embedding tables to represent high-cardinality categorical features such as item IDs (see, e.g., (Covington et al., 2016; Naumov et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2022; Coleman et al., 2023)).
While highly effective at memorizing user-item interactions, this architectural choice hinders the potential benefits of deeper, more complex networks (e.g., (Chen et al., 2019b; Gu et al., 2020)).

The success of LLMs has inspired an emerging paradigm shift for building recommendation models (Rajput et al., 2023; Zhai et al., 2024; Firooz et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2025; Pang et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025).
Consequently, directly applying off-the-shelf LLMs to recommendation tasks has shown a persistent performance gap, even on small public datasets (Hou et al., 2024).

Building on the prior work with RQ-VAE (Rajput et al., 2023; Singh et al., 2024), we introduce a set of new techniques (referred to as SID-v2) for incorporating user behavioral signals and multi-modal content embeddings, and improve the hierarchical integrity through multi-resolution codebooks and progressive masking.

Generative retrieval does not need to maintain a separate index of an item corpus, and bypasses the dot-product limitation (Weller et al., 2025) in embedding-based retrieval (Covington et al., 2016; Yi et al., 2019).

Modeling user sequences and feature interactions have been key areas for improving recommendation models, ranging from using classic sequential neural networks (Hidasi et al., 2016; Kang and McAuley, 2018) to designing custom feature interaction components (Wang et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2024).

More recently, the emerging trend is to use a Transformer-like architecture to unify user history and heterogeneous features in a single sequence (Zhai et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2025; Han et al., 2025), showing better scaling compared to traditional MLP architectures.

Furthermore, the training paradigm itself has evolved to mirror that of LLMs, with some works adopting self-supervised pre-training objectives followed by task-specific fine-tuning (Netflix, 2024; Chen et al., 2025).

Early work demonstrated the feasibility of training retrieval models from scratch to predict SIDs (Rajput et al., 2023), and subsequent research showed that SIDs could be hashed to replace random item ID embeddings, enhancing generalization of ranking models (Singh et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2025).

This includes fusing multi-modal content features (Xu et al., 2025) and injecting collaborative filtering signals from user behaviors (Penha et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025; Yao et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2025).

Different from MMQ (Xu et al., 2025), where different tokens are generated for each modality, we simply concatenate multiple content embeddings before encoding them with an MLP, offering the flexibility of supporting more embeddings.

This idea has gained significant traction across the industry (e.g., (Wang et al., 2025; Mei et al., 2025; Ju et al., 2025; Pang et al., 2025)), since the seminal works in document search (Tay et al., 2022) and recommendation (Rajput et al., 2023).
For instance, OneRec (Zhou et al., 2025) adopts an encoder-decoder architecture to generate video SIDs, and leverages RL training to enhance the model quality with a reward model.
Other works (Yang et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025) propose hybrid models that generate both SIDs and dense embeddings to alleviate the information loss from quantization.
While some research (Cao et al., 2024; Firooz et al., 2025) has explored aligning LLMs with recommendation tasks, their focus is primarily on language interfaces.
A primary limitation of relying on a single content representation in (Rajput et al., 2023) is its inherent inability to capture the multi-faceted nature of complex media items.

• Multi-Resolution Codebooks: Prior work (Rajput et al., 2023) employs a fixed uniform-resolution codebooks that can be parametrically inefficient, leading to a vast and sparsely populated SID space where the majority of potential codeword combinations remain unassigned.
In addition to the training loss introduced in (Singh et al., 2024), we introduce the co-occurence contrastive loss term.
This baseline is the top-performing production model, being highly-optimized since early work such as Chen et al. (2019a).
In Table 4 we discuss the importance of different changes we introduced to the prior SID (Rajput et al., 2023).

We use four different sizes from the Gemini-1.5 (Team, 2024) Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model family: MoE-110M, MoE-370M, MoE-900M, and MoE-3B (here the size indicates the number of activated parameters per token) with their total number of parameters spanning from less than 1B to more than 10B.

Our study was conducted on a production dataset sourced from a key YouTube surface recommending what videos to watch next given a current watched video and other contextual signals like watch history (see Figure 4 in (Zhao et al., 2019)).
Note that unlike scaling law studies in natural language processing (e.g., (Hoffmann et al., 2022)), we employ constant learning rates.
Similar to the Chinchilla paper (Hoffmann et al., 2022), in Figure 6(b) there is a peak for most of the Iso-FLOPS budgets we consider.
